FCC chief Ajit Pai wants Apple to stop disabling FM radio chips in iPhones. Doesn't smartphone FM require a headphone jack for headset wire antenna?

Yes it does, but the antenna on these systems is usually connected to the grounded (reference to phone) shield conductor which is also be carried by the lightning port. The actual headphone connection doesn't matter as long as the shield is present, the connection can be 3.5mm, lightning, or a lightning to 3.5mm adapter. Small cheap portable radios that use headphones are built the same way

That being said, the iPhone uses an Apple custom chipset which may not have the FM tuner function in the first place. If the function is not present, there is nothing to enable. This is likely as the iPhone does not have this function in other markets either where Android phone chipsets typically had this function and was disabled by the US carriers (AT&T started enabling them on all new phones starting in 2016).

This being said the FM radio of a smartphone is not the end all emergency savior that the broadcast industry thinks it is. Here are some limitations of a smartphone FM radio:

  • Requires a wired headset of some kind, a smartphone does is not large enough to have an FM antenna built in. People may not carry this.
  • Control of the radio is provided through the same computer and interface as other functions guzzling power.
  • The FM radio relies on the same battery supply as the rest of the smartphone.
  • A disaster may occur while people are in a building where a headphone cord antenna is very poor.

A better idea is to keep a portable radio set with you in many locations. You don't want anything fancy either. My 1970s Panasonic radio lasts a long time on Alkaline batteries and Sony currently makes a portable that lasts about 10 and a half days (continuously) from 2 D cells. While these aren't pocket portables, they would be okay for a bug out bag.
